The Omnimagnet is comprised of four frames, three solenoids, wire insulation, a ferromagnetic core, cover insulation, insulating paper, and material in the innermost region.
Due to the small size of the Omnimagnet, the Biot number is less than 0.1 for each element, allowing the use of a lumped capacitance thermal model.
The thermal model incorporates conduction, convection, and radiation heat transfer modes, and is represented by a system of ordinary differential equations.
The maximum root-mean-square error between the model and experimental results was approximately 8% (4°C).
The model was optimized by adding correction coefficients to account for uncertainties in dimensions and contact resistances.
The maximum safe operating time and maximum safe input current depend on the size and structure of the Omnimagnet, as well as the lowest melting point of the materials.
Increasing the convection heat transfer coefficient during cooling and at low input currents was found to be an effective method to increase the maximum operational time of the Omnimagnet.
The thermal model was presented in a state-space equation format to facilitate its use in a real-time Kalman filter current controller.

The Omnimagnet is typically a relatively small device, so the transient temperature increase is more important than the spatial temperature distribution, unlike larger devices like power transformers.
The paper discusses the use of modified nanomaterials and magnetic fluid coolants as potential methods to improve the thermal performance of the Omnimagnet.
The Omnimagnet is used for robotically assisted insertion of cochlear-implant electrode arrays, where it is placed adjacent to the patient's head during surgery.
The electrical current flowing through the Omnimagnet's solenoids produces Joule heating, which can lead to device failure if the temperature exceeds the melting point of the wire insulation.
The thermal model was validated against 40 independent experiments on a lab-scale Omnimagnet, with different combinations of powered solenoids and input currents.
The optimization process used a quasi-Newton method to minimize the maximum solenoid temperature difference between the experiments and simulations.
The correction coefficients added to the model ranged from 0 to 1 for the conduction terms, and up to the upper limit for the type of convection used to cool the Omnimagnet.
